book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling

chapters.relation: Editor Nicolas Michaud's introduction argues Deadpool brings an 'obscene number of philosophical questions'—about mortality, morality, the multiverse, killing, and what separates hero, villain, and asshole—and that only waiting for a movie delayed this book. It proposes that philosophers should be more like Deadpool: honest enough to admit no one knows the answers, willing to look into the abyss, laugh, and jump in anyway, and ready to tell unwelcome truths even if it makes them villains. The tone-setting piece closes with bawdy fourth-wall-style gags about the book being 'better than sex' and unlicensed by Deadpool.

chapters.file: ch09 - I. These Timelines Can Get So Confusing Why I Want to Rub Patrick Stewart’s Head.md

chapters.relation: Rhiannon Grant argues Deadpool's fourth-wall breaks make him a great philosopher and sociologist because they enact the examined life: like Socrates's unexamined-life dictum, Deadpool steps outside his world to ask new questions about it ('Stewart or McAvoy?'), and even examines his own habit of examining—the 'sixteen walls' break inside a break. Wittgenstein's fly-bottle becomes the trap of circular philosophical argument that Deadpool escapes by seeing the bottle from outside, while Berkeley's solipsism is the failed attempt to live as if the world existed only in one's mind. A closing dialogue has Professor X coach Deadpool through insider/outsider research ethics and objectivity (the sperm-and-egg microscope example), showing how fourth-wall skill lets a researcher view a community from both inside and outside.

Christopher Ketcham playfully argues that Deadpool's fourth-wall escapes show he exists partly in dimensions we cannot experience, read through string theory's ten curled dimensions and Maimonides's ten realms of angels—beings of form without matter—in the Mishneh Torah. Since only God and angels traverse those hidden dimensions, Deadpool must be an angel, likely a dark one, whose shuttling between realms explains his vacillation between mercenary violence and saving souls. Ezekiel's chariot vision, the vengeful Hebrew Bible God, and massless dark matter are recruited as supporting evidence for this deadpan-earnest science-and-scripture argument.

chapters.file: ch12 - 3. The Only Chapter in This Book You Need to Read!.md
chapters.relation: Writing as two bickering versions of himself from different universes, Karavitis reads Deadpool Kills Deadpool as showing that the multiverse of Deadpools is the delusion of a single narcissist: the alternate 'Pools' are mirror-image projections of himself (Lacan's mirror stage), his self-love is Rousseau's pathological amour propre rather than healthy amour de soi, and his claim to be the progenitor of all reality is solipsism—hence there is no fourth wall. Freud, Fromm, and Marcuse supply rival diagnoses of that narcissism, from arrested development to proto-fascist willfulness to authentic rebellion against social control through unconscious conformity. A closing twist argues philosophers who claim sole access to truth are the same solipsistic narcissists, which would make Socrates, who never claimed a final answer, the only true philosopher.

chapters.file: ch13 - 4. How Much Deadpool Is Too Much Deadpool.md
chapters.relation: The chapter argues Deadpool is entertaining because of, not despite, his excesses: his gratuitous violence and rapid-fire wisecracks breach the disciplined hero ideal, measured against Zeno of Citium's stoic dichotomy of control (accept the torture you cannot change, master your response) and Aristotle's golden mean between deficient and excessive force, which Wade flouts when he savors punishing Ajax instead of finishing quickly. Bakhtin's carnival excess explains the grotesque, orifice-obsessed humor that mocks 'normal' decency, and Derrida's 'internal drifting' (via Poe's Purloined Letter) frames Deadpool's first appearance being FedExed back to sender and his threshold position, where gags spill across comic, game, and film frames—making vigilante justice 'a supplement to the supplement' of law and exposing how each medium works.

chapters.file: ch14 - II. I’m No Hero Seriously, Why Do We Like This Guy He Has No Redeeming Qualities Other than a Moderately Sized.md

chapters.relation: Andy Vink applies Joseph Campbell's hero's journey, in the Power of Myth version where heroism is a transformation of consciousness from selfishness to self-sacrifice, to the Duggan-Posehn arc 'The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly'. Deadpool starts self-centered—demanding pillowcases of money for killing zombie Presidents—is transformed by revelations (Dr. Butler holding his daughter Eleanor hostage, the North Korean mutate experiments echoing his own Weapon X trauma), and ends risking himself to free Butler's sister and the captive mutates and their families. The verdict: Deadpool genuinely becomes a hero by Campbell's test, which is also why, in Campbell's scheme, the hero never gets the girl.

Darian Shump judges Deadpool by Buddhist lights, applying karma as intentional action and skillful means—the permissibility of compassionate killing, after Rupert Gethin—to his Marvel NOW! career: protecting Agent Preston, saving a child and Nightcrawler Kim mid-battle, and the Niagara Bride assisted suicide whose fee he donates to a home for kids with cancer. A hypothetical Hydra spy with a bomb on a S.H.I.E.L.D. helicarrier shows how killing one murderer-to-be can be the compassionate act that saves everyone. He concludes Deadpool is an 'accidental hero'—a mercenary first whose good intentions make him a karmic hero—while Zenpool's failed pacifism in AXIS shows that renouncing violence betrays what makes Deadpool Deadpool.

chapters.file: ch17 - 7. Why Deadpool Isn’t a Hero (Yet ).md
chapters.relation: Matthew Brake maps Deadpool onto Kierkegaard's three spheres (aesthetic, ethical, religious) and argues Wade is stuck in the boundary zone of humor between the ethical and the religious: his comedy sees the contradictions between everyday life and the heroic ideal but revokes suffering in jest, instead of embracing it as essential the way the religious hero does. Spider-Man is the contrast case—wisecracking as the incognito of inner suffering over Uncle Ben and Norman Osborn—while Deadpool's healing factor and knowledge of his own fictionality let him laugh off decapitation ('RESPAWN. LOL') and regress from every heroic step. The chapter ends with Wade's plan to earn heroism in Spider-Man/Deadpool #1 undercut by his taking a contract on Peter Parker.

chapters.file: ch18 - 8. How Shitty Can a Hero Be.md
chapters.relation: Corey Horn maps the Deadpool movie onto Joseph Campbell's monomyth—ordinary world, call to adventure (the cancer diagnosis), refusal of the recruiter's offer, acceptance, and the ordeal of hunting Ajax—then asks whether a mercenary chasing reward can be a hero at all. MacIntyre's chess example distinguishes instrumental from intrinsic rewards of a practice, and Kant splits motivation into duty versus self-interested motives; since Wade hunts Ajax to recover his face and Vanessa, both thinkers would deny his journey is moral. Still, MacIntyre's allowance for migrating from instrumental to intrinsic motivation leaves Deadpool a hero-in-progress, already promising Colossus he will consider joining the X-Men.

chapters.file: ch19 - III. Wade, Is That You Is It Just Me Who’s Getting Tired of That F$ %ing Avocado Joke.md
ch20 - 9. Is Headless Deadpool Still Deadpool.md
chapters.relation: Ben Fulman runs Deadpool's decapitations, the T-Ray personality split, and Evil Deadpool—his discarded body parts regenerating together in a dumpster—through the theories of personal identity: Locke's memory continuity, Reid's branching-memory 'Deadpool paradox', Chisholm's essential parts, the Ship of Theseus traced from Heraclitus to Plutarch, and later positions by Sider, Wiggins, Noonan, Grice, and Perry on overlapping memory chains and their circularity. Finding each account strained by Deadpool's cases, the chapter proposes that Deadpool stores his memories in the readers via the fourth wall. His identity over time is thus jointly sustained by the audience—a 'non-personal identity' that ends only when every reader has forgotten him.

chapters.file: ch21 - 10. Always a Pallbearer, Never the Corpse.md
chapters.relation: Heidi Samuelson argues Deadpool is Camus's absurd hero improved: his origin and his survival of impossible dismemberments embody the absurd as 'disproportion between intention and reality', and facing Camus's one real philosophical problem—suicide—he tries to die via the Hulk to join mistress Death yet must live on, rejecting both actual and 'philosophical' suicide (dogma). His mercenary sense of purpose, jokes in the face of oblivion, and compassion for Blind Al, Weasel, deaf Hawkeye, and Evan exemplify Camus's revolt, freedom, and passion. Sisyphus is the model: like him, Deadpool owns his rock—the healing factor and the killing—and is happy, laughing where Sisyphus is silent.

In dialogue with Deadpool himself, John Altmann tests whether immortality is a blessing: Bentham's utilitarianism would prize a healing factor that lets Wade dive into a gamma meltdown to save the Southern Hemisphere for free, and Nietzsche would hail him as an Übermensch for refusing the Mithras Directive's Messiah and preserving humanity's freedom to create its own values rather than adopt herd morality. Bernard Williams gets the last word: since personalities become fixed—Wade stays a mercenary across every run, Zenpool notwithstanding—an endless life curdles into boredom and misery, so immortality is punishment rather than power unless one could radically change who one is.

Chad William Timm argues Deadpool is not really insane but was made 'insane' by power: via Foucault's genealogy of madness, experts like Dr. Brighton (a robotic shell for Psycho Man) at Ravenscroft and Dr. Whitby at Crossmore, along with the courts that institutionalize him after the Hulk trial, run a knowledge/power nexus that labels, sorts, and disciplines him until he internalizes the madman identity ('I think I might actually be crazy'). Nineteenth-century psychiatry's invented link between crime and madness secured the experts' authority, and disciplinary power plus technologies of the self made Deadpool discipline himself. Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe's 'I can see through the bull##$%' and his fourth-wall awareness become resistance to these regimes of truth, and the chapter closes by turning Socrates's examined life on the reader: be careful whom you tell.

Cole Bowman argues Deadpool is the Marvel Universe's deus ex machina: phenomenologically alienated from a body he treats as a prop (cutting off his own hand to escape Colossus's manacle and flipping the silver behemoth the bird), he can step outside the causal chain the way Leibniz's Primary Truths says any genuinely free agent in a created order must. Sartre supplies the engine—radical freedom against determinism, with She-Hulk's shallow fourth-wall gags (killing the already-dead Porcupine) as bad faith by contrast and Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe as the extreme exercise of freedom against his creators and fans. Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy account of the deus ex machina replacing metaphysical consolation frames this new kind of inside-the-story god, who complicates plots rather than conveniently fixing them.

chapters.file: ch25 - IV. Looks Aren’t Everything Why Ryan Reynolds Can’t Act.md

chapters.relation: Daniel Alloy argues Deadpool keeps insisting 'I'm an X-Man!' because being a hero is not a private choice but a social standing: with Aristotle's beast-or-god line about those who cannot live in society and Hegel's account of mutual recognition in the Phenomenology of Spirit, he contends Wade needs heroes he recognizes to recognize him as one in return. The Thunderbolts ('the selfish Avengers') and X-Force recruited him as a merc and so could not grant that recognition, and Cable offers approval from superiority rather than recognition between equals—a friendship of utility where Wade wants one of virtue. Only Captain America's Avengers card treats him as an equal, and even that recognition must be completed by the whole hero community before Wade can accept himself as the hero he already is.

holes.name: Amour Propre (pathological self-love)
holes.what: Rousseau's term for comparative, status-hungry self-love that seeks superiority over others, as opposed to healthy self-preservation (amour de soi).
holes.why: Chapter 12's central diagnosis of Deadpool as malignant narcissist rests on Rousseau's amour propre versus amour de soi distinction (alongside Freudian narcissism), and the taxonomy has no slug for either.

holes.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
holes.what: Russian philosopher of the carnivalesque: licensed bodily excess, grotesque humor, and inversion of hierarchies as subversive social release.
holes.why: Chapter 13 explains Deadpool's orifice jokes, grotesque masks, and boundary-overspill through Bakhtin's carnival excess (Rabelais and His World), a framework the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Joseph Campbell
holes.what: Mythologist of the 'hero's journey' (monomyth): a universal narrative arc in which the hero is transformed from self-centeredness into self-sacrifice through trials and revelations.
holes.why: Chapter 15 tests Deadpool's arc in 'The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly' entirely against Campbell's Hero of a Thousand Faces and The Power of Myth.

holes.name: Skillful Means (upaya)
holes.what: The Buddhist principle that a normally wrong act, even killing, can be right when performed out of compassion to prevent greater harm.
holes.why: Chapter 16 justifies Deadpool's killing of the Hydra spy and the Niagara Bride contract through upaya, a concept the taxonomy lacks despite its karma and compassion slugs.

holes.why: Chapter 18 reads the Deadpool movie stage by stage through Campbell's monomyth (ordinary world, call, refusal, reward) before turning to MacIntyre and Kant.
